articles.title_orig: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.title_zh: At least 68 people dead in Spain's second major train crash this year
articles.content_orig:
At least 68 people have been killed and dozens more injured after a Spanish high-speed train collided with another train south of the capital Madrid
The updated death toll makes this crash the country's worst rail disaster since 2013
Spain's transport minister says an "inexplicable" decision by the control centre led to the collision after a computer failure initially caused trains to halt
The rail operator Iryo says its train was "struck from behind" by a Renfe train. More than 500 passengers were travelling on the two trains
Speaking at the crash site, Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez says Spain is "grieving" - most major parties have suspended general election campaigning
SÃ¡nchez also vows to find out "why this tragedy occurred" - here's what we know so far about the cause
Witnesses have described "terrible" scenes , while Roberto GÃ³mez, a Spanish journalist travelling on one of the trains, says it was "extremely chaotic and very distressing"
Edited by Craig Hoyle and Europe digital editor Paul Kirby, with teams reporting from Spain
Spanish trade union CSIF is demanding the resignation of Transport Minister Ãscar Puente following today's high-speed train collision.
In a statement, it accuses Puente of "scapegoating" a traffic manager during his press conference earlier today instead of "taking responsibility".
"The minister has shirked all responsibility despite the initial computer system failure that triggered the events," CSIF adds.
Earlier, we brought you comments from the transport minister in which he said it was "inexplicable" that a control centre allowed the high-speed train to start moving again after a computer failure, when another train was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
Transport Minister Ãscar Puente speaks at a press conference earlier
Salvador Arriza, 62, says that the fact that he was travelling in the opposite direction to the train he was on saved him from being thrown out, like other passengers.
"I was very close to the door, but [other passengers] were breaking the windows to be able to get out," he tells Reuters.
The 62-year-old describes scenes of wreckage, with seats ripped out through the carriage where he was sitting near the back of the high-speed Renfe train.
"Some people practically couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats," he says.
Rafael BarcelÃ³ was travelling in the high-speed AVE train that crashed.
He says he was in the cafeteria car and that may have saved him and a friend from suffering the worst of the impact.
âWe were having breakfast, having a coffee and we felt a huge impact, we were all thrown into the air," he tells Reuters, with a visible wound on his forehead.
"I am reasonably OK, my friend is quite worse.â
Their seats were in car number seven, "which is the one with more victims and the one most destroyed," BarcelÃ³ says.
"I at least counted eight victims in that coach."
As we've just reported, rescue personnel are working into the night at the scene of the crash near Spain's capital of Madrid.
In its most recent update on social media, Spain's interior ministry says there are 102 people from Spain General Secretariat for Civil Protection and Emergencies are on site.
A further 422 personnel from the Guardia Civil are also assisting, along with three helicopters, and drones and dogs.
Nick Beake Europe correspondent
Transport Minister Ãscar Puente
The most significant information today has come from the Spanish transport minister who said that from his perspective - looking at the information available so far - this incident was due to human error.
He described a situation just before 09:00 local time this morning, where there had been a computer failure which had led to at least six services in the area being halted.
But then a decision was made to give the go-ahead to one of these high-speed trains to continue its journey, which led to the crash.
Spain's transport minister said this decision was "inexplicable" and there was no clear rationale why it was made.
One development that's being reported in the Spanish media is that the Guardia Civil have apparently been interviewing everyone who was in the main control centre in Atocha, in Madrid, at the time this decision was made to tell the high-speed train to continue its journey.
The train that was hit from behind was still stationary when the order was given to the other train to proceed.
According to regulations, under such circumstances, a train driver would be required to proceed at what is known as "sight speed" - about 40km/h (25mph), a speed that allows them to stop in time if they encounter an obstacle.
Officials will investigate what order the Renfe train got, if it was travelling at the usual speed for that section of track - "around 200km/h" according to the minister, and, more significantly, why did the operator not stop its journey when his screen would have displayed that another train on the same line was stationary.
Affected passengers were visibly angry.
"It isn't possible that our train was stopped for five or 10 minutes and that the other train wasn't told to stop," one of them said.
"How can this happen with the technology we have?"
The latest images from the crash site show a continued effort by emergency workers to clear up the wreckage.
Lights have been deployed as dusk falls, while a large crane is also at the scene.
Earlier, local authorities confirmed that the bodies of 68 victims had been recovered from the crash site.
Spain's Civil Guard says its "top priority" is to identify relatives of the train crash victims using DNA samples.
Four offices for relatives have been set up in Madrid and other parts of Spain, according to the force.
So far, Spanish authorities have confirmed 68 people died in the crash, with dozens more seriously injured.
Isabel NÃºÃ±ez is a local councillor in Urda, close to the crash site, who has been helping receive injured people at the town's sports hall.
She tells BBC Mundo that people with minor injuries, such as cuts or bruises, have been picked up by family members or transported back to where they live by bus.
Some people were "very dazed" and "were completely in shock" when they arrived, Isabel says, adding "many didn't even know which carriage they had been travelling in".
She goes on: "Urdaâs two local police officers were among the first to arrive at the scene of the accident.
"This morning we have seen everything. A man arrived on a motorbike, completely disoriented, looking for his wife, who had been on the train. He was desperate.
"We also helped a man with a head wound who had left his carriage to stretch his legs and was saved because of that.
"His carriage was the one that caught fire and where most of the victims were. He was relieved and grateful to be alive, but deeply saddened by the whole situation."
European leaders have shared their condolences and willingness to support Spain following the train collision.
Elizabeth Conway BBC Sport Spanish football reporter in Madrid
People wait in Madrid to donate blood
I've just stepped outside in Madrid to find a queue of more than 100 people waiting to donate blood in the city centre.
The donation van is usually parked on Gran VÃ­a, Madridâs main shopping street, where there are normally only a handful of people waiting. Iâve never seen a queue anything like this before.
In coffee shops today, the train crash was all anyone seemed to be talking about.
Thereâs a real sense of shock and heartbreak across the city, with people sharing news and information about whatâs happened on social media.
Due to the volume of donations, Madrid president Isabel DÃ­az Ayuso is asking others to "wait until tomorrow and the following days, when it will still be just as necessary".
Spanish PM Pedro SÃ¡nchez says the government is working "to clarify what happened, why this tragedy occurred". Here's what we know so far:
Guy Hedgecoe Reporting from Urda

articles.title_orig: Fed Chair Warsh says central bank to reduce the number of rate-setting meetings in coming years
articles.title_zh: Fed Chair Warsh says central bank to reduce the number of rate-setting meetings in coming years
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve plans to eliminate some meetings devoted to setting interest rates in the next couple of years, Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
Starting next fall, the central bank will dedicate one of its eight annual meetings to considering broad-based questions about the economy, rather than to voting on interest rates, Warsh said. That number will increase to two in 2028.
The chairman made the announcement following the release of the central bank’s latest policy announcement, which left rates unchanged .
He said the rationale for doing so was to devote more time to thinking about longer-term issues by shifting attention away from the immediate interest-rate environment.
“Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals,” he said. “But it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons.”
Warsh’s announcement marks a major shake-up for the Federal Reserve’s long-standing policy calendar, which is closely watched by investors around the world. The Federal Open Market Committee has held eight scheduled meetings a year since 1981.
Warsh began seriously discussing a reduction in rate-setting meetings in July, according to the FOMC’s meeting minutes, arguing that a longer lag between rate-setting meetings would allow the committee to accumulate more data about the economy.
Reducing the number of rate-setting meetings has long been debated over concerns about shortsightedness — but the switch was never enacted over fears that the Fed would become less nimble in reacting to sudden changes in the economy.
The change would make the Fed unique among major central banks, including the Bank of England and Bank of Japan.
It marks another major change enacted by Warsh, who took the reins of the Fed in May after being nominated by President Donald Trump.
Warsh has dramatically shortened the FOMC’s post-meeting policy statement. He has also declined to issue what is known as “forward guidance,” which contains forecasts about future inflation and unemployment.
Rob Wile is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist covering breaking business stories for NBCNews.com.

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash kills at least 68 as witnesses describe devastating scenes
articles.content_orig:
The horrific crash south of Madrid was caused by human error after a computer system failure, officials say
• Deadly rail crash: Scores of people have been killed and about 100 injured after a high-speed train collided with a stationary train south of Madrid. Spain’s transport minister called it “inexplicable” that a train was allowed to continue its journey despite a red signal being in place.
• ‘People were hurled into the air ’: Several witnesses told CNN about the chaotic moment when passengers were thrown airborne during the collision. Rescue operations are still ongoing and the high-speed line linking Madrid with Andalusia remains suspended.
• Third train crash this year: This is the third rail disaster in Spain in 2026. In January, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz , in southern Spain’s Córdoba province, killing more than 40 people. A commuter train near Barcelona derailed days later.
• Sigue nuestra cobertura en vivo en español
Ana has been searching for her husband, Pepe, all day. But so far, no luck.
She raced to Madrid as soon as she heard about Wednesday’s deadly train collision in the Spanish province of Toledo, she told Reuters. Pepe was traveling on the high-speed Renfe train that crashed into the stationary Ilyo train while heading from Madrid to Seville.
Ana, who only provided her first name, told Reuters that Pepe’s name was not on the list of victims who have been identified.
Local police did however find Ana’s dog, who had been traveling with Pepe.
“Poor thing, I think he’s had a bad time,” she told Reuters, speaking from a school in Urda – the town closest to the site of the train crash – where relatives have been advised to wait.
Renfe, a state-owned railway company, said it had opened a special phone line for families of victims, Reuters reported.
In the days ahead, investigators in Spain will continue to gather details to understand what exactly led to the deadly train collision that killed at least 68 people, said Janos Rozsa, a railway accident investigator and safety specialist.
Spain’s transport minister said the was crash caused by human error after a computer system failure, but Rozsa said “accidents rarely have a single cause.”
Incidents like this “usually result from a combination of different contributing factors that are present at the same time,” he told CNN’s Isa Soares.
Officials will use things like surveillance cameras and data recorders on the trains and on the signaling system to piece together how the trains were moving and how they ended up on the same piece of track.
While human error may be one part of the what caused the crash, it will also be important for investigators to fully understand “the circumstances in which people were working and how the overall system was designed to keep these trains apart.”
While this is the third rail disaster in Spain this year, Rozsa said it is too early to draw any conclusions if the incidents had any common threads.
Scores of people were killed after two trains collided in Spain on Wednesday, in a crash that authorities say was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error.
Spain’s transportation minister Óscar Puente said that a computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically.
At that point, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, ADIF, took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound along the tracks despite a red light.
The Renfe train was authorized to proceed without any speed restrictions due to an erroneous order from a train controller. As a result, Puente said that between 8:36 a.m. and 8:52 a.m. local time, it resumed traveling at about 124 miles per hour, eventually colliding with the stationary Iryo train.
You can read more about the circumstances of the collision here .
Night has fallen in Spain and crews are working against the clock to find anyone who is trapped in the rubble after Wednesday’s deadly train collision.
More than 500 emergency personnel have been deployed to the site of the crash Wednesday’s deadly train collision, the Spanish Interior Ministry said.
The Civil Protection has sent 102 people while the Civil Guard has deployed 422 personnel and 123 resources, the ministry added.
Crews are also using three helicopters, several drones, cavalry, dogs, an advanced command post, and citizen assistance offices.
The Civil Guard said investigators are using drones to create a 3D reconstruction of the area and determine the accident’s possible causes.
Right now, crews have bright flood lights set up at the site so that they can keep working all night, CNN correspondent Pau Mosquera reported from the scene.
Of the at least 68 people who died in Wednesday’s horrific crash, at least 24 were traveling on the high-speed AVE train and 44 people were found on the stationary Iryo train, the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha said.
The AVE train, operated by the state-owned Renfe railway company, had 393 passengers on board when it collided with the Iryo train, which had 151 passengers.
There are currently more than 100 people with injuries of “varying severity,” the regional government added.
Authorities say they have deployed “all the means and resources” at their disposal to deal with the emergency.
“Several” US citizens were injured in the train crash in Spain, a US State Department spokesperson told CNN.
They did not provide specific details on the number of Americans hurt in Wednesday’s deadly train crash, which has killed at least 68 people.
“The Department of State and the US Embassy in Madrid are working closely with local authorities to assist Americans following the train collision,” the spokesperson said. “We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of all those affected.”
CNN saw US embassy officials at the scene of the collision in Spain’s Toledo province.
The spokesperson noted that Americans in need of consular assistance, or with concerns about American loved ones in Spain, can contact the State Department 24/7 at +1-202-501-4444 from abroad or +1-888-407-4747 from the US and Canada.
“We encourage US citizens in the area to notify loved ones of their safety and monitor local media for updates,” they said.
A surviving passenger from Spain’s deadly train crash has described scenes of chaos as she tried to assist fellow travelers to safety.
Three train cars were in “terrible shape,” Eduarda Contreras told CNN. “One was on fire, in another there were people trapped and crying … And then in the main one (impacted) – there were people buried under debris, people who are probably dead.”
Other passengers were trying to break the train’s windows to escape, she said.
Contreras recalls being told not to let injured passengers fall asleep while assisting in rescue efforts before help arrived. “They told me, ‘Stay with them, don’t let them fall asleep – they’ll die, they’re slipping away.’”
Spain’s King Felipe VI has conveyed his condolences over today’s deadly train crash in the Spanish province of Toledo, saying he shares in the “sorrow of the families and loved ones” of the deceased.
The social media post said the royal family’s support goes out to the emergency teams involved in the recovery effort and “all those working in the area to help as much as possible under these circumstances.”
CNN’s Duarte Mendonca contributed reporting.
After a host of European leaders offered their condolences for the victims of the deadly train crash in Spain this morning, other international leaders are also expressing their solidarity today.
An erroneous order from a train controller, following a signaling system failure, resulted in Wednesday’s deadly train crash, according to Spain’s transport minister.

articles.title_orig: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.title_zh: Wendy’s, struggling with beef prices and growing competition, gets a buyout offer
articles.content_orig:

Struggling burger chain Wendy’s has received a buyout offer from noted investor Nelson Peltz.
The buyout offer comes after Wendy’s shares dropped roughly 70% over the past five years, per the Wall Street Journal. Peltz argues that the fast food giant would be better off as a private company and offered to pay around $1.4 billion.
The chain, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. Same-store sales, or sales at restaurants open at least a year, have declined for more than two years. Those sales fell during the first two quarters of 2026.
Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday.
Restaurant operator Flynn Group and investment firms BlueFive Capital and Sixth Street Partners have partnered with Trian on the offer, according to WSJ .
In a letter to the company’s board of directors, Peltz said going private “will deliver the best outcome for the broader stakeholder base.”
“Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture," Peltz wrote. "The external environment has become increasingly challenging given the significant pressures on the U.S. consumer, economic uncertainty, persistent commodity inflation and intensifying competition, particularly within the QSR (quick service restaurant) burger category."
Peltz has invested in companies from Procter & Gamble and Disney, to DuPont. According to a regulatory document filed Wednesday, Trian’s stake in Wendy’s totals 16.3%.
Wendy’s, based in Dublin, Ohio, didn’t immediately comment. Restaurant industry heavyweight Robert Wright took over as the chain’s new president and CEO in May, replacing interim boss Kenneth Cook.
Wright previously ran sandwich chain Potbelly Corp and held top leadership roles at Wendy’s, Domino’s Pizza and Charleys Philly Steaks. He said in August that Wendy’s needs to improve its food, prices, customer experience and marketing to win customers back.
Wendy’s is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results next week. Analysts expect Wendy’s earned 9 cents per share on sales of $531 million on average.
Shares rose 91 cents to $7.05 Wednesday.

articles.content_orig:
Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.
Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30,  compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.
Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.
Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.
Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.
Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.
Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.
Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.
—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran rejects "unacceptable" ideas as Qatari mediators say they presented new draft deal to Tehran
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran rejects "unacceptable" ideas as Qatari mediators say they presented new draft deal to Tehran
articles.content_orig:
Qatari mediators on Sunday handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war, the Reuters news agency reported, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Tehran is considering the proposal and set to respond by the end of the week, the agency reported Wednesday.
The source added that there were concerns in Tehran before the meeting on Sunday that Israel could resume its bombardment of Iran this week.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

Israel ’s election has ended in a deadlock as no party is on track for a majority of the Knesset , exit polls have suggested.
The stalemate comes after three years of war waged in Gaza , Lebanon and Iran , which have plunged the Middle East into turmoil.
The election is widely seen as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu , who is seeking another term after a combined 19 years in power .
But now, the jostling for power between parties to achieve a governing coalition and name the next prime minister could take weeks or even months.
There are 38 different parties contesting the election, but most will not get enough votes to secure one of the 120 seats in the Knesset.
Israeli elections are based on nationwide proportional representation. Citizens cast votes for a single party – not for individual candidates – and the party’s number of seats is determined by the proportion of the national vote it receives.
To actually enter the Knesset, a party must receive at least 3.25 per cent of the vote, or four seats.
Historically, no single party has won a majority, ​so governments are formed by a coalition. If no one manages to form a coalition with a 61-seat majority, citizens return to the ballot box.
Polls opened at 7am local time and closed at 10pm that night (8pm GMT). An exit poll by Israeli TV channels revealed the initial results, but the official, full results will not be confirmed until Tuesday 4 November.
However, the whole process will take much longer, ranging from 20 to 100 days. In the past two decades, no government has been sworn in in less than 50 days.
After a coalition agreement is signed, the Knesset convenes a special session during which the designated prime minister presents the new government and its policy agenda.
A formal vote is then held, and if the new government wins the vote, it starts its tenure.
The election is viewed domestically as one of the most consequential in the history of Israel .
The outcome could have profound consequences for Palestinians and Israel’s relations with neighbouring states, as well as international partners like the US and Europe.
Some of the main issues centre on the debate over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews , how the state should investigate its inability to prevent the October 7 2023 Hamas attacks and future concessions in Gaza , the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.
Israel’s wars have also put pressure on the economy, so the cost of living will definitely weigh on people’s minds when casting their votes. For context, the state’s defence budget has doubled since 2023.
Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of far-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, and the other camp is led by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defence Forces.
The current exit polls released by major Israeli TV stations suggested that Netanyahu’s bloc won 50 seats, the opposition won 52-53 and Arab parties won 17-18.
Dr Nimrod Nir, of Agam Labs, said that “the real political drama will begin the morning after the election”.
“Israel’s election is not a single game, but a tournament – and election day is only the opening round,” he added.
“Our polling suggests that neither bloc is likely to secure a governing majority, leaving three possible outcomes: a unity government bringing Netanyahu together with more liberal parties, an alternative coalition backed by Arab parties, or yet another election.”

articles.title_orig: Why China is desperate to ship cars overseas
articles.title_zh: Why China is desperate to ship cars overseas
articles.content_orig:
To understand why China is desperate to ship cars overseas, visit a dealership in Beijing.
Autumn has traditionally been the peak time to buy vehicles in the country, but this year many showrooms are empty or shut.
Car salesman Li Ke said that other than the Covid-19 pandemic, the 2026 "golden September and silver October" season, as it's known, is the slowest he's seen in his 26 years on the job.
"In past years, customers would come to the showrooms nonstop," he told CNBC during an interview in his deserted showroom at a complex of dealerships on the outskirts of the Chinese capital. "We would have deals to sign every day. But nowadays we see only two to three deals a week. It's a dramatic drop."
Many people in China aren't buying cars because an unstable job market and a continued slide in property prices have undercut consumer confidence. The government has also scaled back incentives such as cash-for-clunkers subsidies and tax breaks to go electric, car salespeople said.
Passenger car retail sales for 2026 in China totaled 13.33 million units through September, falling 21.7% from a year ago, according to the China Passenger Car Association. For the full year 2026, China's domestic passenger car retail sales are set to drop 22% to 18.5 million vehicles, the association said — under the level recorded in the first year of the pandemic.
Even electric vehicles, which were once a bright spot, are down. Gasoline car sales have been declining in China because of the country's transition to electric vehicles, but sales in China of new-energy vehicles — which includes EVs — dropped by 12.8% from January through September, according to the association.
"Customers are watching every penny," Li said. "When looking at all the new functions on all these new models, they are weighing what is most practical, economic and worth their money over the long term. We don't see impulse buying. Because of the bad economy, people are taking more time to replace their cars."
The fierce competition has led to bruising price wars in recent years, a key reason Chinese carmakers have cast their eyes overseas and why Beijing is fearful of partners like the U.S. and Europe putting up coordinated trade barriers against its massive car exports, analysts said.
Industrial profits for the first nine months of the year were up 15.5% from the same period in 2025, but September showed signs of weakness relative to the prior eight months, according to China's National Bureau of Statistics . For the auto manufacturing industry specifically, profits from January to September shrank by 22.8% compared with last year.
To preserve cash, Li's dealership moved out of a pricey streetside space to one with less foot traffic but that rents at a fraction of the cost.
With profit margins eroding, Li said he sees little point in offering further discounts. He said the bigger hurdle is the prevailing Chinese consumer attitude toward big-ticket purchases.
"Chinese buyers would rather wait," he said.

articles.title_orig: Apple Unveils Touch-Screen MacBook Pro, Reversing Longheld Jobs Stance
articles.title_zh: Apple Unveils Touch-Screen MacBook Pro, Reversing Longheld Jobs Stance
articles.content_orig:
Apple on Wednesday announced its first laptop with a touch screen, which it is calling MacBook Pro with ProLED XDR Display.
Apple said that the laptop has a new display, using OLED technology, that offers more brightness, better colors and wider viewing angles. It's using Apple's M5 Pro or Max chips, and Apple said on Wednesday that it's lighter than Apple's current pro laptops.
It's still an Apple laptop, and is running MacOS, not a version of the iPhone or iPad operating system. In a video, Apple showed users swiping on the screen to manipulate videos or images. It also has a glowing Apple logo on the laptop's lid.
The new laptop will go on sale on Nov. 6 and the 14-inch version will start at $2,899. The 16-inch version will cost at least $3,399. Both are notable price increases from existing models.
This is Apple's third major product launch under new CEO John Ternus, signaling a faster cadence for hardware releases. It's also a major reversal for Apple, which has resisted putting touchscreens on its laptops for decades as some Windows machines gained the feature.
"Yes, for the very first time, we are bringing touch to the Mac," Ternus said in live remarks to media and analysts in Los Angeles.
The new MacBook Pro comes at a time when the laptop market has been going through one of its worst slumps ever. Overall shipments are expected to be down 11% this year. Analysts say the AI-driven global market shortage of memory has contributed to higher laptop prices, which has hurt sales and demand.
In the third quarter, total PC shipments dropped 20% on a year-over-year basis, according to market researcher IDC. Apple's own shipments fell 11% during the quarter, according to the estimate.
Even Apple's not immune to rising memory prices, after former CEO Tim Cook warned this summer that the situation around memory prices was "unsustainable." Nearly all Macs got price hikes this year. Mac Minis introduced in August got a $300 bump, for example.
The announcement caps a busy two months of product launches under Ternus.
Apple also introduced new iMac and MacBook Pro models with M6 chips this week, after price hikes to the lineup totaling several hundred dollars in June. Apple introduced an iPad Mini on Monday that starts at $699, $100 more than its predecessor.
In September, Apple released new iPhones, including its first foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. It also revealed a new smart speaker with a display called HomeView that uses a redesigned version of Siri to answer a broader range of questions.
The launch signifies the growing strategic importance of the Mac to Apple, despite it generating less revenue than the iPhone. In the most recent quarter, Apple reported $10.35 billion in Mac sales, or just under 10% of the company's total revenue.
But many software developers swear by the Mac, and it remains the only supported platform to develop iPhone apps. And in recent months, Apple has highlighted its chips and memory architecture to make the case that its computers are the best fit for local or edge AI that runs on a device, instead of the cloud.
Meta's AI model developer team bought hundreds of Mac Minis this year to test agents, for example. And Apple notably teamed up with Meta earlier this month to make an announcement that large, nearly frontier models can run on clusters of Macs connected with high-speed cabling, allowing developers to run agentic code without paying Anthropic or OpenAI.
Apple has had a historical resistance to touchscreen laptops — software chief Craig Federighi explained in 2018 that the ergonomics would fatigue users. "We make the world's best touch computer on an iPad. It's totally optimized for that. And the Mac is totally optimized for indirect input. We haven't really felt a reason to change that," Ternus, then Apple's senior VP of hardware engineering, told The Wall Street Journal's Joanna Stern in 2021.
Ternus has been working on Macs since he joined the company and was credited along with silicon chief Johny Srouji as the leader of Apple's effort to get Macs running on Apple's chips, not Intel's. Apple credited Ternus' work on Mac in its official CEO transition statement .
That may be why Ternus in his early days as CEO will be the executive to backtrack on a long-running Apple design philosophy.
Touchscreen laptops have been available on Windows machines for a long time, but they're just another feature, not a selling point behind most purchasing decisions, Ryan Reith, IDC VP for worldwide device trackers, said.
Only 17% of notebook PCs shipped globally this year will have touchscreens, according to IDC data. Touchscreen laptops also have a slightly lower average selling price than non-touchscreen notebooks.
Hardware technology hasn't been the limiting factor for Apple merging its desktop and mobile interfaces, he added, and Apple could have been waiting to launch a touchscreen laptop until it could present a good user experience and perfect its software after attempts to make its iPad more like a laptop.
"This is really a user interface and software thing," Reith said. "It's one more thing that can draw the developers in."

articles.title_orig: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.title_zh: China-Vatican deal has imperfections, Vatican’s foreign minister says
articles.content_orig:
Archbishop Paul Gallagher acknowledged the agreement’s challenges in a meeting with journalists in Rome.
Archbishop Paul Gallagher, the Vatican’s secretary for relations with states and international organizations, acknowledged the challenges of the Vatican-China deal on Tuesday.
Speaking at an event with journalists in Rome, the British diplomat responded to questions regarding the agreement, Pope Leo XIV’s health, and calls for a ceasefire in the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war.
The full text of the 2018 agreement between China and the Holy See has never been made public. Under the publicly understood terms of the agreement, the pope retains final authority over episcopal appointments in China and may reject candidates proposed by Beijing. The Holy See, for its part, agreed not to appoint bishops without the Chinese government’s prior approval.
As reported by Reuters , Gallagher said that, regarding the agreement, its imperfections were visible.
“Itʼs not easy, the dialogue is not easy,” Gallagher said. “The imperfections of the agreement are ⁠evident, but ​there is a commitment to persevere in dialogue ... and that is what will ​continue to happen.”
He also answered questions regarding a potential visit from Leo to the U.S., saying that it could happen “in the not too distant future.”
Regarding the pope’s Oct. 13 surgery and subsequent recovery, Gallagher described it as a “bit of a game changer” and a revelation of the pope’s mortality, as with every human being.
“[The pope] is a poor mortal like the rest of ​us,” Gallagher said.
In August, Gallagher traveled to Russia to discuss the country’s ongoing war with Ukraine with senior officials. He told journalists that he did not believe the Vatican was involved in discussions of the ceasefire between the two nations.

articles.title_orig: Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation
articles.title_zh: Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold, opting to take a patient approach in its fight against inflation despite mounting evidence that price pressures are proving more nettlesome than policymakers had hoped.
In a widely expected decision, the Federal Open Market Committee kept the overnight funds rate in a range between 3.75%-4%, where it has been since the central bank approved a quarter percentage-point increase in September.
"Inflation remains elevated," the post-meeting statement said . "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."
Two of the 12 FOMC voters dissented from the decision – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, both of whom wanted the committee to raise rates by a quarter percentage point.
Cook has been at the center of a continuing controversy in which President Donald Trump has tried to remove her from office over allegations concerning information she provided on home loan applications. While the Supreme Court stopped the president's attempts, the administration has restarted the move, with a hearing scheduled in early November .
This was Cook's first dissent since joining the Fed in 2022 as an appointee of President Joe Biden.
Dallas President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis President Neel Kashkari both joined Hammack in voting no the last time the committee held, in July, and both have expressed the need for higher rates. However, they fell in with the majority Wednesday.
The midterm elections have lingered over the decision. Pivotal votes take place nationwide on Nov. 3, with control of Congress at stake. Fed officials consider political independence to be a cornerstone of the central bank, but some observers have speculated that officials won't want to raise rates this close to an election.
Trump, who nominated Warsh to the position, has been at odds with the Fed for years. Trump has charged that the funds rate should be much lower.
The dissents reflected underlying conflict on the committee over how aggressively it needs to raise rates to combat rising prices. Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and the pace of price increases has only picked up since the September meeting.
Statements over the past several weeks, though, have reflected a desire to wait for additional data to come in before tightening policy further. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams both said current economic conditions allow policymakers time to evaluate their next move.
The statement characterized economic activity as "expanding at a strong pace," a seeming upgrade from "solid" in September. There were no other substantial changes to the statement other than the removal of a sentence that explained the September increase.
The decision came as little surprise as markets had been pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool . Following the decision, the S&P 500 held on to its gains .
However, it raises fresh questions about how long policymakers are willing to wait before tightening again. Futures market pricing indicates a strong possibility of another hike at the next FOMC meeting in December, and perhaps another hike or two in 2027.
Separately, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh unveiled at a news conference changes to the FOMC meetings next year that could reduce the number of rate-setting meetings each year.
"We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said. "The rest will be regular FOMC policy setting meetings, and I expect that in 2028 we'll have two meetings dedicated discussions of strategy and six for setting policy."
The Fed is up against a complicated economic and political picture. Inflation as measured by the Fed's preferred gauge is expected to be above 3% for September, even when excluding volatile food and energy prices. Economists are concerned that inflation has broadened beyond the energy sector and the impact from the Iran war.
At the same time, the unemployment rate has remained low and economic growth has been strong. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker is pointing to 3.4% annualized growth in the third quarter, which would be the strongest in a year. Consumer spending also has been solid, and investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom has helped keep the U.S. economic engine running.
The combination, though, has added to debate about how much restriction the Fed's current interest rate is actually exerting on the economy, and whether policymakers will need to move more aggressively if the price data doesn't improve.
While markets expect additional hikes, Warsh has avoided providing so-called forward guidance about the FOMC's intentions. In June, his fellow committee members, through the "dot plot" grid, indicated the likelihood of another increase this year.
"The Fed is taking a wait-and-see approach, and I think that makes sense given where we are in the cycle," said Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust and a former BLS analyst. "...The economy is slowing, but slowing and breaking are two different things. Holding rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess how the economy is responding to September's hike and the recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs."

articles.title_orig: Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform
articles.title_zh: Google adding more Connected Apps to Gemini & Search with new dev platform
articles.content_orig:
Google today announced the Connected Apps Platform as a “unified way for more app developers to bring their capabilities directly into Gemini and Search.”
Existing third-party Connected Apps let you access Adobe, Dropbox, Instacart, OpenTable, Ticketmaster, and other services — now numbering over 50 — from the Gemini app. Google also announced a new Calm integration that will be available in the coming weeks. These @-integrations join first-party offerings like Google Workspace, Photos, and YouTube. To date, the creation process has required working closely with Google.
Google is now expanding availability on multiple fronts, starting with the Connected Apps Platform. It’s billed as a way to “build once and reach high-intent users.” Developers need to have a cloud-hosted MCP server or Android MCP using the AppFunctions APIs. They then register, test, and submit their Connected Apps using the new Google Connected Console. This new website lets them track traffic, latency, and error rates, as well as control brand identity.
In addition to the Gemini app, Google will soon make existing Connected Apps available in Search. Developers can “choose whether [their app] will go live in Search, the Gemini app, or both.” As part of the recent redesign, the Gemini app gained a new Customize page .
Developers can sign up for the preview at developers.google.com/connected-apps . Google is opening up access in phases over the coming months.

articles.content_orig:
Nintendo’s latest Indie World presentation has just finished, and we’ve got the full details below.
The show featured a total of 23 games over the course of its 15-minute runtime, showing a selection of indie games coming to Switch and Switch 2 .
Here’s the full list of everything announced, in the order it was announced, with accompanying trailers.
Wizarding school life sim Witchbrook is coming to Switch and Switch 2 on January 28.
Winds of Viridia is an action adventure game coming to Switch 2 in early 2027, with a free demo available later today.
“The expansive single-player journey features fluid combat, unique creatures, and majestic bosses, set to an original soundtrack from award-winning composers Kevin Penkin and Christopher Larkin ,” its description reads.
“Players will encounter lost towns, make strange new friends, battle fearsome foes, discover ancient lore, and uncover what is driving the wild beasts of these forgotten lands mad.”
City of None is a new retro-style platformer from one of the co-creators of Celeste , featuring a stylised four-colour palette. It’s coming to Switch and Switch 2 in 2027.
“A metropolis crumbles into ruin as powerful Barons feast on souls lost in time,” its description reads. “You are but one spirit, with a wooden body left to rot in the wild. Will you seize back your city’s future?”
Critically acclaimed 2025 adventure game Sword of the Sea is coming to Switch 2 tomorrow, October 29.
Tenjutsu is a “gritty combat roguelike” described as a “love letter to action games” from the designer of Dead Cells . It’s coming to Switch 2 in 2027.
“Trapped in this purgatory, use your martial arts mastery and weapon expertise to wipe the slate clean for yourself and the people of Secret Garden by dismantling each of the unique syndicates one at a time, in whatever order you wish,” its description says.
Threads of Time is “an epic, epoch-spanning, turn-based RPG inspired by timeless classics”. It’s coming to Switch and Switch 2 in Summer 2027.
Dumpster Gang is an online co-op sandbox game for up to four players about raccoons causing havoc at night. It’s coming to Switch 2 in March 2027.
Super Battle Golf , an 8-player cross-platform online golf game where everything takes their shots at the same time, is coming to Switch 2 on March 25, 2027.
R.E.P.O. is an online co-op horror game where you repossess items from haunted houses. It’s coming to Switch 2 in 2027.
Haunted Paws is a co-op adventure about two puppies rescuing their human friend from a haunted mansion. It’s coming to Switch and Switch 2 in May 2027, with a free demo available today.
Kitsune: The Journey of Adashino tells the story of a fox girl and her frog companion exploring a mysterious island wrapped in darkness. It’s coming to Switch and Switch 2 in Spring 2027.
Slime Rancher 2 is coming to Switch 2 in January 2027.
Spirit Crossing is a collaborative life sim MMO. It’s a Switch and Switch 2 console exclusive, released on November 16.
My Arms are Longer Now is an Australian comedy game where you play as an extremely long arm trying to rob everyone. It’s coming to Switch and Switch 2 on March 11, 2027.
Petal Runner , the retro-inspired adventure game about life and loss, is coming to Switch 2 on March 8. A free demo is available today.
Raccoin : Chaos Max Edition is coming to Switch 2 on November 10. The Chaos Max Edition adds eight characters with their own gameplay modifiers. A free demo is available later today.

articles.title_orig: Palantir Board Member Cofounded Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner’s Blood-Testing Startup
articles.title_zh: Palantir Board Member Cofounded Elizabeth Holmes’ Partner’s Blood-Testing Startup
articles.content_orig:
Billy Evans has spent the past week as the breakout character of the year’s most talked-about documentary. Now attention is turning to his day job.
Evans, the longtime partner of convicted Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, runs Haemanthus, an Austin-based startup that says it can use lasers to detect disease in blood, saliva, and urine. Interest in the company has surged since A24 released You Can See Everything , Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the couple, on Oct. 16.
Haemanthus has reportedly raised as much as $20 million and holds at least one granted patent. What it doesn’t have, at least publicly, is a product customers can buy or published data showing its technology works. It has also lost its chief technology officer .
Set aside the “Theranos 2.0” jokes, and a more basic business question remains: What has Haemanthus actually built?
Evans, 34, is a grandson of William and Anne Evans, who founded Evans Hotels in San Diego in 1953. The privately held, family-owned company operates three resorts in Southern California. But in an Oct. 1 statement, Evans Hotels said Billy Evans is neither an employee nor a shareholder .
Evans graduated from MIT in 2015 with a degree in economics. After a stint at LinkedIn, he worked as a special projects manager at Luminar Technologies, a lidar startup building sensors for self-driving cars, from 2017 until January 2019, according to Forbes . His LinkedIn profile has since been scrubbed of every job except Haemanthus. Luminar filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 2025, nearly seven years after Evans left.
Evans met Holmes at a party in 2017, when Theranos was already engulfed in scandal. They have two children, William, 5, and Invicta, 3. Evans refers to Holmes as his wife, but Holmes told People that the couple never legally married. “Maybe we’ll get married someday, but our bond is more than a piece of paper,” she said.
Evans has listed himself as Haemanthus’s CEO since October 2022. According to marketing materials reviewed by the New York Times last year, the company’s device uses a laser to scan biological samples “on a molecular level,” identify biomarkers such as glucose and hormones within seconds, and use AI to detect cancer and infections.
The underlying technique, Raman spectroscopy, is not new. Shining light on a sample and reading the signal that scatters back is a long-established way to identify chemicals. Forensic investigators use handheld Raman devices to identify suspected drugs at crime scenes, and labs can analyze substances through plastic bags or glass without opening them.
Blood is a much harder problem. The molecules researchers want to detect are often present in tiny amounts, so their signals are faint. Other components in blood can produce stronger signals that drown them out, according to a scientific review published in Applied Spectroscopy .
That approach is also what separates Haemanthus from Theranos. Holmes’s company claimed it could run conventional lab tests on a miniaturized machine using a few drops of blood. “Theranos attempted to miniaturize existing tests,” Haemanthus wrote on X in May 2025, describing its own approach as fundamentally different.
A Raman spectroscopy patent assigned to Haemanthus and granted in January 2025 names two inventors, one of them former CTO Joseph LaChapelle, according to Forbes . Several of the startup’s early staffers, including LaChapelle, worked with Evans at Luminar, NPR reported . Eric Potma, a UC Irvine chemistry professor who consults for the company, told Wired that the concept isn’t pulled out of thin air, though he declined to go into detail because of his advisory role.
A patent, however, does not establish that a test can accurately diagnose patients.
Haemanthus plans to start with veterinary testing before pursuing human applications. That market is far less regulated. The FDA does not require premarket approval for devices intended for animals, though it can take action against misbranded or adulterated products.
According to investor materials the Times reviewed last year, Haemanthus initially raised $3.5 million from friends and family. In spring 2025 it began approaching wealthy investors in Austin and the San Francisco Bay Area for another $15 million. The materials described an eventual wearable device for humans that would take three years and $70 million to develop. Wired has since reported that the company has received as much as $20 million.
A person who spoke with Evans this spring told Forbes that Evans said early Palantir employees had invested.
The company has yet to launch a commercial product or disclose independently validated diagnostic results.
LaChapelle told Forbes he left in March. “I resigned on March 16, 2026, due to a conflict of interest associated with a stealth startup I had founded prior to Haemanthus,” he said, declining to elaborate.
Evans has told it differently. The same person who spoke with Evans this spring told Forbes that Evans said he had let the CTO go. That person also recalled Evans describing the company as “Theranos 2.0,” a label Haemanthus has publicly rejected. Evans did not respond to Forbes’ s request for comment.
Holmes is serving an 11-year sentence for defrauding Theranos investors at a federal prison camp in Bryan, Texas, roughly a two-hour drive from Austin.
Citing two sources with direct knowledge, NPR reported in May 2025 that Holmes had been advising Evans from prison, though the nature of that advice was unclear. Haemanthus denied it on X , saying Holmes had “zero involvement” and “no role, now or future.” Wired reported that Holmes’s name does not appear in Haemanthus’s incorporation documents.
The documentary muddies that picture. It shows Evans and Holmes on fundraising calls and discussing a medical-testing venture, and Evans tells Fielder, “The idea is to put the band back together and do it all again.” Forbes noted it’s unclear whether those calls were for Haemanthus or another venture. A source close to Evans told New York magazine that the project in the film was separate from Haemanthus. According to that source, it aimed to make medical testing cheaper without conventional chemical methods and was shelved when a panel of tests still cost several hundred dollars.
Evans has acknowledged the film may backfire. Speaking at the All-In Summit before he had seen the finished cut, he said, “I might think this is like the dumbest thing I’ve ever done.”
The documentary reveals that Evans asked for a share of its profits, a request that worried the filmmakers about their independence. Fielder says they reluctantly agreed. A postscript says Evans ultimately decided not to accept payment.
That may not be the end of it. Page Six Hollywood reported on Friday, citing unnamed sources, that Evans has been seeking Hollywood legal representation over a possible cut. One prominent litigator reportedly declined to take the case, and a source said Evans might donate any proceeds to charity.
The film has put Holmes back in the spotlight. Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz and Bad Blood author John Carreyrou have both weighed in, and Fortune has questioned whether her new persona distracts from the real story . It has also drawn far more scrutiny to Evans and Haemanthus. The company has yet to publicly show that its technology can reliably detect disease. It also remains unclear when its veterinary device will reach the market or how close its larger ambitions are to reality.

articles.title_orig: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.title_zh: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.
The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.
He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.
Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.
"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.
"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.
"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.
"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."
Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.
It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.
Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .
Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.
"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."
Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.
"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.
At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.
Burnham's comments at Prime Minister's Questions came as a letter emerged addressed to his Cabinet ministers, asking them to be "aligned and disciplined" around the summit.
"It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process," he wrote in a letter on Wednesday.
He said he hoped the summit led to "some important, concrete steps" and he would set out the next steps "to consider the UK's long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan".
"Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote," he said.
"Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality."
Any "fundamental change" to this relationship "would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next Parliament," he added.

articles.title_zh: Epileptic woman dies after going to ChatGPT for medical advice; family files lawsuit against OpenAI
articles.content_orig:

The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported .
Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.
The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety . A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives .
In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.
The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.
The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.
ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.
The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.
In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.
When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.
The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.
Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence.
Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not.
Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”
Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”
At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery.
The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”
Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.
The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.
OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.
Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits.
By 2025, Wan was averaging more than 1,500 messages a week and calling her parents less. “Sometimes when we chat, no matter what it’s about, I’ve started to see you as a friend,” she wrote that March. “Once she had ChatGPT,” Qun Wan said, “she didn’t talk to us as much.”
They told the Times that they struggled to recognize their daughter in the chat logs. Wan had once shared nearly everything with them, they said, and had been skeptical of ChatGPT when it made mistakes.
“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”

articles.title_orig: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.title_zh: Spain Train Crash Live Updates: At Least 68 Killed in High-Speed Train Collision, Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
Toledo, Spain 6:07 p.m. Oct. 28
A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another in Spain on Wednesday morning near the central city of Toledo, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens more, officials said, in one of the deadliest train crashes in Spanish history.
The cause of the crash, which sent parts of both trains down a rural embankment, was not immediately clear. It was the second lethal crash this year involving the same two rail operators, and it was likely to deepen doubts about the security of Spain’s once-vaunted rail system.
In Spanish news reports, passengers described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.
The crash also came about a month ahead of national elections, and it had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s left-wing government.
Sixty-eight people were seriously injured in the crash, 15 of them critically, said Emiliano García-Page, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region.
Spain’s rail authority, the Adif, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company,” both covering the route between Madrid, the capital, and the southern city of Seville. Renfe is the national rail provider.
Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.
Trains from the same operators collided on a southern line in January, leaving 46 people dead.
Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said on Wednesday that initial reports indicated two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed. He said all traffic on the Madrid-Andalusia route had been suspended until further notice.
Mr. Sánchez visited the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon, saying that Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced. “If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” He declared three days of official mourning.
The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern.
“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media soon after the crash. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.” His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.
Another deadly crash: In January , a northbound Iryo train derailed, two of its cars falling onto the opposite track, and a southbound Renfe train slammed into the carriages seconds later. An official report on what caused that lethal accident has not been released, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause.
A detailed account: In a news conference, Spain’s transportation minister described the events that he said preceded the crash on Wednesday.
José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.
The U.S. State Department said in a statement that several U.S. citizens were among those injured in the crash. It did not provide information about their conditions.
Spain’s transportation minister said a train crash that killed dozens on Wednesday appeared to result from an “inexplicable” decision by traffic control operators to tell a high-speed train to continue its journey when another train was stopped farther along the tracks.
The minister, Óscar Puente, said he spent the morning watching a reconstruction of the accident and listening to audio recordings of communications between the control center in Madrid and the trains that crashed near Toledo, and he gave a detailed account of what he said preceded the crash at a news conference.
At about 8:30 a.m. local time, an automatic train control system near the site of the crash went down because of a computer failure, Mr. Puente said.
The system — known as the Linienzugbeeinflussung or LZB — dates to the 1960s and uses external technologies, such as track circuits and axel counters, to monitor the speed and position of trains. This information allows the system to automatically calculate when and how quickly a train can safely move forward. It then changes railroad signals accordingly.
On Wednesday, the safety system was inactive along a stretch of about 39 miles, or 63 kilometers, of tracks, so six trains traveling along that section were automatically stopped as a precaution. At that point, he said, the control center in Madrid took over.
“The control center communicated with the trains that had stopped, and at 8:36 a.m., the decision was made to allow the train that eventually collided with the stationary Iryo train to resume its journey as normal,” Mr. Puente said, referring to the private rail operator of the stopped train.
Traffic controllers working for Adif, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s rail infrastructure, told the train that eventually rear-ended the other to restart its planned journey, Mr. Puente said, “despite there being another train ahead of it.”
The train that was hit from behind was believed to have received instructions from traffic operators to continue, he said, but for unknown reasons it did not proceed.
The moving train then hit the stationary train.
“And that is the origin of the accident that has taken place,” Mr. Puente said, adding that the moving train should have been stopped according to protocol.
The Madrid-Seville route is currently undergoing a modernization program that will replace the LZB system with the more modern European Rail Traffic Management System. Infrastructure officials hope that the new system will cut down on human error in signaling.
Mr. Puente also said that the driver of an uninvolved train tried to warn the control center of the dangers when its operators greenlit the rear train’s resumption of its journey. That driver told the control center operator that trains should proceed at lower-than-normal speeds. The operator, Mr. Puente said, acknowledged his error. “Oh, yes,” the operator replied.
K. R. Callaway contributed reporting.
When the crash happened, Yahadi Mohamed Maulud, 41, who lives in the nearby town of Yébenes, loaded his car with water bottles and rushed to help. “We found a massacre,” he said, describing torn limbs and a blood-covered woman searching for her brother. One of the first to arrive at the scene, he helped to move injured passengers and carry stretchers. Mr. Maulud said he often took the train himself to Madrid for business, but no more: “I’m never getting on that train again.”
So many people showed up at Madrid hospitals on Wednesday to donate blood for victims of the train crash that the authorities are asking citizens to wait until Thursday or the following days, when more donations will be needed.
“The response from the people of Madrid to the call for blood donations is overwhelming,” said Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Madrid’s regional president. “Thank you, everyone.”
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez spoke from the scene of the crash on Wednesday afternoon. “It’s not possible for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed train accidents in one year,” he said, adding that while today’s accident and a fatal January crash on the same line seemed unrelated, Spanish rail’s security systems clearly needed to be reinforced.
“If there has been negligence, it will come to light,” he said. “If there have been failures in the safety system, we will respond with the utmost firmness.” Spain needs to understand “what is the origin of this tragedy,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.title_zh: Chinese astronomers find planets that somehow avoided death by red giant stars
articles.content_orig:
Study suggests the long-term fate of the solar system, including Earth, ‘may be far more complicated than predicted’, according to scientist
When a star like our sun grows old, it puffs up into a red giant that can gobble up its nearest planets.
But Chinese astronomers say they have found three solar systems where planets should have been eaten this way yet somehow survived – a puzzle that could change how scientists picture Earth’s distant future.
Using Nasa’s TESS space telescope, a team led by Qian Shengbang from Yunnan University showed that three Jupiter-like planets – each hugging an ageing star in the northern sky – had lived through their hosts ballooning out past them before shrinking back.

The leader of a Weil Gotshal & Manges practice group told his junior lawyers to look for employment, underscoring the firmâs perilous state as it consults with a restructuring lawyer.
Alex Lynch, who leads Weilâs capital markets group, communicated the news to associates in a group meeting Tuesday, a person familiar with the announcement said. He said the associates will remain employed for the time being and will continue to work on client matters, though he offered no specific timeline on their tenure, said the person, who requested anonymity to describe Weil communications.
Lynch and Weil did not respond to a request for comment.
The firmâs future existence is uncertain after a litany of partners fled, at least in part because of a lack of confidence in Weilâs leaders. Last month powerful corporate department chairman Michael Aiello moved toward an exit for rival Cravath, and a wide set of firm partners learned last weekend that incoming Weil leader Ramona Nee has decided not to take the job.
Davis Polk & Wardwell lawyers, including restructuring partner Brian Resnick, are advising Weil as it assesses its future, two people familiar with the matter said Tuesday. Resnick is head of Davis Polkâs liability management and special opportunities practice.
The storied New York-based firm, with more than 1,200 lawyers and $2 billion in revenue, has long been one of the USâs premier legal operations. It is renowned for its bankruptcy practice, acting as lead debtors counsel to Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc and Enron Corporation . It also was an M&A powerhouse, led by Aiello, who represented Fox Corp. on its $22 billion acquisition of Roku Inc.
Aielloâs departure along with others prompted the firm to explore its options, including a possible merger with another Big Law firm. But merger talks with Willkie Farr & Gallagher fell through last week, raising questions as to whether a dissolution is the inevitable option.
